analysis.title: The Fed's Unpaid Intern: MS' Wilson Says Tighter Financial Conditions Are Already Doing Warsh's Job (Just Not To The AI Generals)
key_insights: Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson argues tighter financial conditions across rates, the dollar and oil are doing part of the Fed's work. Weak breadth in economically sensitive areas shows it, while index-level performance does not, because the largest AI-centric weights are less sensitive to oil and cost of capital.

MS composite of financial conditions (52-week z-score averaged across rates, the dollar and energy) is about 1.4 standard deviations, a level breached only a handful of times in 35 years, most recently in 2022.
The FOMC hiked 25bps to 3.75-4.00% last month. Goldman penciled in a second hike for October.

Of the ~130bp rise in the 10-year since February, ~120bp came through real yields. Equities have historically absorbed breakeven-led rises more easily than real-yield-led ones. Wilson says the risk is the pace of the move from here, and another real-yield-led spike in bond vol would be the harder outcome.
Wilson says 10Y yields above 5% are not outrageous with trailing 10-year nominal GDP growth near 6%. The article reads this as 5% on the 10Y looking more like a floor than a ceiling.
S&P 500 Equal-Weight has lagged Cap-Weight by 6% over six months. In September, when the 10Y moved above 5%, equal-weight fell 5% while cap-weight was roughly flat.

Over the trailing 30 days only TMT and Energy are positive among S&P sectors. Healthcare -3.5%, Consumer Discretionary -3.6%, Utilities -4.6%, Industrials -5.8%, Financials -7.7%, Materials -7.9%, REITs -9.8% (zerohedge tweet).
Per zerohedge, 85% of S&P 500 names are more than 10% below all-time highs, 59% more than 20% below, 41% more than 30% below, 26% more than 40% below and 17% more than 50% below.

Wilson's breadth gauge: share of S&P members above their 200-day moving average fell to 43% at end of September, below the late-March low of 44%, then recovered to 50%. Forward P/E retested its March low near 19x.

Wilson says the de-rating has run ahead of any earnings deterioration, the classic mid-cycle combination. His equity risk premium framework puts fair value at ~19.6x vs 19.2x today, so equities do not need a large bond rally if yields consolidate.

The article notes the S&P 500 equity risk premium (forward earnings yield minus the 10Y) has slipped below zero, a level barely visited since 2002. Stocks are cheap versus a model that assumes yields stop rising, and expensive versus bonds.

Wilson sees no migration from a valuation problem to a growth problem yet: nominal GDP printed 8.5%, median stock earnings growth is in the mid-teens, fed funds less core CPI is about 1.4%, 10s2s is about +45bp and the 2-year is about 90bp above fed funds. He says growth deterioration within 12-18 months is rare under these conditions.

Wilson's two tells are relative performance of Financials (called perhaps the most important for near-term equity direction) and bond volatility (MOVE). MOVE surged above 110 in late September. Both show some stabilization but need more follow-through. Financials relative to the S&P are near their lowest since at least 2019.
Goldman's Privorotsky observed longer-dated bond vols have retraced roughly 30% of their recent move.

Upcoming tests: September CPI on Wednesday, Warsh fireside chat at the IMF on Thursday, and the October 28 FOMC. Consensus sees headline CPI +0.6% MoM on a 9.6% gasoline jump, taking the annual rate to 3.6%.

Goldman's Pasquariello pushes back on the breadth concern: the median S&P stock trades 15% below its 52-week high (worst since the dot-com bubble), but S&P, NDX, RTY and SPW are up double digits YTD, all but two sectors are higher YTD, nearly 2-in-3 S&P names are positive, 123 names are up 25%+ vs 42 down 25%+, and 53 are up 50%+ vs 8 down 50%+.

Pasquariello says positioning is light: Goldman sentiment indicator negative six straight weeks, GS prime book net exposure in the 10th percentile of the past year, and last week's S&P breakout came with client turnover ranking 49th of 52 weeks. Today's session traded on the lowest volume in 23 years.

Pasquariello's call is to stay short fixed income and stay long NDX. He flags 2027 as setting up to be complicated, with lockup expirations potentially sending net US equity supply up the most since 2000.

Wilson's recommendation: stay with quality but broaden. Add risk through higher-quality cyclicals. Capital Goods stands out, with revisions breadth improving from 16% in February to nearly 40%. Base case is a S&P target of 8,300.

sector_views.rationale: Morgan Stanley remains overweight Financials. Wilson says their relative performance is the key near-term tell for equities, and they sit near the lowest relative level since at least 2019.
Wilson favors higher-quality cyclicals. Revisions breadth improved from 16% in February to nearly 40% as manufacturing backlogs broaden across machinery and fabricated metals.

earnings_insights: Median stock earnings growth is running in the mid-teens per Wilson (Morgan Stanley). Big banks begin earnings season on Wednesday Oct 14. Wilson says the equity de-rating has run well ahead of any deterioration in earnings.

tension_points.bull_case: Wilson and Goldman's Pasquariello argue conditions are not as dire as they look. The de-rating has run ahead of earnings, and Pasquariello notes major indices are up double digits YTD, 123 names are up 25%+ versus 42 down 25%+, and positioning is light. Wilson's base case is Warsh blinks, yields consolidate, Financials turn and the average stock catches up, with an 8,300 S&P target.
tension_points.bear_case: Tightening is real but absorbed by everything except AI-weighted index leaders. Financials are near their relative lows since 2019, the equity risk premium is below zero, and a hot CPI could keep Warsh from relenting. Real yields spiking again and bond vol re-erupting would pull the index down to its members.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financials failing to stabilize and a renewed real-yield-led spike in bond volatility (MOVE back above its late-September 110+ level), or a hot September CPI followed by no acknowledgment from Warsh at Thursday's IMF fireside chat.
